stages.name: Observe
stages.instruction: Drag a resistor cartridge into the empty slot and move the voltage slider $E$. Watch the ammeter reading $I$ and the growing $I(U)$ scatter plot. Try at least two different resistors and two different voltages. The lamp cartridge is non-ohmic — note how its trace differs.
stages.concept: Ohm's law for a resistor: $U = R \cdot I$, so $I = E / R$ when the battery is ideal. On the $I(U)$ plot the resistor traces a straight line through the origin whose slope is $1/R$. The lamp is not ohmic — its trace curves.

stages.name: Experiment
stages.instruction: Hit both target readings shown top-right. Pick the correct resistor and adjust $E$ until the ammeter reads the target current within tolerance. Order does not matter.
stages.concept: For an ideal battery, the voltage across the resistor equals the source voltage: $U = E$. So $I = E / R$. To read $I = 100$ mA through $R = 47\,\Omega$ you need $E = R \cdot I = 4.7$ V.

stages.name: Evaluate
stages.instruction: The $I(U)$ scatter on the left shows measurements taken with an unknown resistor. Read the slope, compute $R = U / I$ on paper, then drop the matching cartridge from the restricted palette into the empty slot. One attempt.
stages.concept: Slope of the $I(U)$ line is $1/R$. Pick any point $(U, I)$ on the line and use $R = U / I$. All points lie on the same line for an ohmic dipole — pick the one that reads most cleanly.

labels.place_resistor: read the slope · pick the resistor
labels.tip1: drag a resistor into the slot; move the E slider; watch the ammeter and the plot
labels.tip2: R sets the slope; E sets the operating point on that line
labels.tip3: compute R = U / I from any point on the plotted line
labels.peek_tip: Slope of the I(U) line equals 1/R. Pick any point, then R = U / I.

1.1: Drag a resistor cartridge into the empty slot on the right side of the circuit.
1.2: Move the E slider up and down. The ammeter reading changes proportionally.
1.3: Swap in a different resistor. Both traces are straight, but their slopes differ. The steeper slope is the smaller R.

2.1: Read each target: it fixes both the resistor value and the target current.
2.2: Ohm's law rearranged: E = R times I. For 100 mA through 47 Ohm, set E = 4.7 V.
2.3: Place the required resistor, then nudge E in 0.1 V steps until the ammeter is within tolerance of the target.

3.1: Look at the scatter plot on the left. All measurements are on a straight line through the origin — that means one resistor.
3.2: Pick any point on the line. Read its U and its I. Compute R = U / I.
3.3: If R comes out near 100, the answer is 100 Ohm. Match to the closest cartridge in the palette.
